Multilevel latent class analysis with the latents R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/lca.Rmd
lca.Rmd

Latent class analysis (LCA) is the categorical-data counterpart of latent profile analysis, extending the person-centred approach to situations in which the observed indicators are categorical rather than continuous. Whereas latent profile analysis identifies subgroups based on differences in the means of continuous indicators, LCA identifies latent subgroups based on differences in the probabilities of endorsing or selecting particular response categories across a set of categorical items. Each latent class is therefore characterized by a specific configuration of item-response probabilities, representing the likelihood of observing each response category conditional on membership in that class (Collins & Lanza, 2010). The resulting classes can be interpreted as distinct response patterns that capture unobserved heterogeneity in the population.

Two-level latent class analysis extends this framework to hierarchical data structures in which individual observations are nested within higher-level units, such as students within classrooms, employees within organizations, or patients within healthcare institutions (Vermunt, 2003). In conventional LCA, individuals are assumed to originate from a single population characterized by a common set of class proportions. However, when observations are clustered, the distribution of individual-level latent classes may differ across groups. Two-level LCA accounts for this possibility by introducing a second latent classification at the group level. The model consequently distinguishes between individual-level classes, which describe differences in response patterns, and group-level classes, which capture differences in the composition of those individual-level classes across groups.

For observation ii belonging to group jj, let CijC_{ij} denote the individual-level latent class and GjG_j the latent group class. The model estimates three sets of parameters that jointly describe the individual and group classifications.

First, the item-response probabilities, defined as θkqc=P(Yijq=c∣Cij=k)\theta_{kqc}=P(Y_{ijq}=c\mid C_{ij}=k), describe the probability of observing response category cc on item qq, conditional on an individual’s membership in class kk. These probabilities determine the substantive characteristics of each individual-level class by describing its characteristic response pattern. An important assumption of the two-level specification is that these item-response probabilities remain invariant across group classes. Thus, an individual belonging to a particular latent class is assumed to exhibit the same conditional response probabilities regardless of the group to which they belong.

Second, the individual-level class probabilities, expressed as πk∣m=P(Cij=k∣Gj=m)\pi_{k\mid m}=P(C_{ij}=k\mid G_j=m), represent the probability that an individual belongs to class kk, conditional on the membership of their group in group class mm. These probabilities describe the composition of each group class in terms of its constituent individual-level classes. For example, different group classes may be characterized by different proportions of individuals exhibiting particular response patterns, even though the underlying item-response probabilities defining those individual-level classes remain unchanged. The probabilities sum to one across the individual-level classes within each group class.

Third, the group-level class probabilities, defined as ωm=P(Gj=m)\omega_m=P(G_j=m), represent the proportion of groups belonging to each latent group class. These parameters describe the distribution of the higher-level latent classes across the population and determine the relative prevalence of the different group types.

The distinction between the two levels of classification is important for interpreting the model. Individual-level classes represent subgroups of observations characterized by similar response patterns, whereas group-level classes represent subgroups of higher-level units characterized by different distributions of individual-level class membership. Consequently, two groups may belong to different group classes even when the same individual-level classes are present in both. Their distinction lies in the relative proportions of individuals belonging to each class rather than in differences in the response probabilities defining those classes. This allows the model to identify systematic differences in group composition without requiring the individual-level measurement structure to vary across groups.

The two-level LCA specification relies on several conditional independence assumptions. First, the observed categorical items are assumed to be locally independent conditional on individual-level class membership. This means that the association between items is assumed to be explained by the underlying latent class, such that no additional residual association remains between the indicators after conditioning on class membership. Second, observations within the same group are assumed to be independent conditional on their group’s latent class. Their responses may therefore be associated at the population level through their shared group classification, but are treated as conditionally independent once that classification has been taken into account. Finally, groups are assumed to be independent of one another. Together, these assumptions establish the hierarchical structure through which individual response patterns and between-group differences in class composition are modelled simultaneously.

In the latents package, the function multilca() estimates the two-level latent class model using maximum likelihood estimation and the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977). The algorithm alternates between estimating the posterior probabilities of latent class membership and updating the model parameters until convergence is achieved. As in multilevel latent profile analysis, the estimated individual-level classes are labelled profile_1, profile_2, and so forth in the model output. These labels are used for consistency across the package’s modelling functions and do not imply that the classes are based on continuous indicators. The same naming convention is used in multilpa(), facilitating a consistent interpretation of individual-level latent classifications across categorical and continuous measurement models.

Data

student_esm comes from an experience-sampling study of university students (Neubauer & Schmiedek, 2024) and contains 2,582 prompts from 100 students (15 to 51 per student), answered when the student had not studied since the previous prompt. Prompts are the observations and students the groups. Eight yes/no items record leisure activities since that prompt; four ratings from 1 to 7 record affect; ?student_esm describes the source and the selection of prompts.

library(latents)
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
summary(student_esm)
#>     student           day             beep      time_with_friends on_social_media tv_video_games

Social media is the most frequent activity (745 of the 2,582 prompts), followed by TV or video games (549); a part-time job is the rarest (103). Every activity is absent at most prompts, so classes are distinguished by how far their “yes” probabilities exceed these base rates.

A first model

multilca() treats every item in vars as categorical. n_starts sets the number of random starts and tol the convergence tolerance; a strict tolerance is required for accurate standard errors. A first model has two classes and two group classes.

first <- multilca(student_esm, vars = activities, id = "student",
                  n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 20,
                  tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)

Number of classes

enumerate_classes() fits every combination of two to four classes and one to three group classes, each from twenty random starts, and get_results(candidates, "best") reports the candidate that each criterion selects.

candidates <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, vars = activities,
                                categorical = activities, id = "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:3,
                                n_starts = 20, tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)
#> 2 of 9 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (classes3_groups3, classes4_groups3); refit those you consider with more starts.
get_results(candidates, "best")
#>    criterion  convention        candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15126
#> 2        kic        <NA> classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15172
#> 3        bic      groups classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15238
#> 4        bic individuals classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15377
#> 5      sabic      groups classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15102
#> 6      sabic individuals classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15241
#> 7       caic      groups classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15281
#> 8       caic individuals classes4_groups3          4               3  <NA> 15420
#> 9        awe      groups classes3_groups2          3               2  <NA> 16767
#> 10       awe individuals classes3_groups2          3               2  <NA> 16956
#> 11       icl      groups classes3_groups2          3               2  <NA> 16546
#> 12       icl individuals classes3_groups2          3               2  <NA> 16641
#> 13       clc      groups classes3_groups2          3               2  <NA> 16413
#> 14       clc individuals classes3_groups2          3               2  <NA> 16413

The BIC (Schwarz, 1978) decreases up to the largest model in the grid, four classes and three group classes; that model and the one with three classes and three group classes reach their best log likelihood from a single start, as the message reports, so their low BIC rests on solutions that the starts do not replicate. The ICL (Biernacki et al., 2000), AWE (Banfield & Raftery, 1993) and CLC, which penalize uncertain classification, select three classes and two group classes, a model whose best solution is reached by two of the twenty starts. compare_models() sets the two-class model beside the three-class model.

lca <- multilca(student_esm, vars = activities, id = "student",
                n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 20,
                tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)
compare_models(two = first, three = lca)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model  Classes  Group classes   k    LogLik       BIC   ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8  Group entropy  Group min AvePP
#> -----  -------  -------------  --  --------  --------  -----  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----  -------------  ---------------
#> two          2              2  19  -7739.84  15567.19  77.35   0.000  16762.74     0.67       0.86      0           0.88             0.96
#> three        3              2  29  -7678.14  15489.84   0.00   1.000  16640.78     0.80       0.86      0           0.88             0.95

The third class lowers the BIC by 77 and the ICL by 122, and raises relative entropy from 0.67 to 0.80. The three-class model is retained.

The chosen model

The classes describe three kinds of leisure interval. Class 2 (71.6% of the prompts) is low activity: no activity exceeds a probability of 0.17. Class 3 (24.9%) is media use: social media (0.792), TV or video games (0.397) and music (0.366). Class 1 (3.5%) consists of the prompts at which the student worked in the part-time job (probability 1.000), with almost no other activity. get_results(lca, "responses") returns the same probabilities as a table, and the response plot compares them across classes.

plot_responses(lca)

The activity items have “no”/“yes” labels, so the response plot is the appropriate view. For items with distinct, finite numeric category labels, such as ratings from 1 to 5, plot_profiles() summarizes each item’s distribution in each class by its probability-weighted mean, or by its median or mode (statistic = "median" or "mode"). Means assume meaningful spacing between the category scores. The median is the smallest score whose cumulative probability reaches 0.5, and tied modes take the smallest score. These summaries use the fitted probabilities, including in FIML models, rather than averages of the cases assigned to each class, and they are on the raw scale. They have no confidence intervals and therefore do not require the parameter-inference calculation of the response plot. In mixed models, plot_profiles() shows only the continuous indicators.

Group classes 

get_results(lca, "profile_probabilities")
#>   group_class profile probability group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1     0.00778                   0.436
#> 2           1       2     0.46348                   0.436
#> 3           1       3     0.52874                   0.436
#> 4           2       1     0.05862                   0.564
#> 5           2       2     0.92787                   0.564
#> 6           2       3     0.01351                   0.564

The group classes are kinds of students. In group class 2 (56.4% of the students), 92.8% of the prompts fall in the low-activity class, 5.9% in the job class and 1.4% in the media class. In group class 1 (43.6%), the prompts divide between media use (52.9%) and low activity (46.3%). The two kinds of students therefore differ in media use rather than in activity overall. The prevalence plot shows these probabilities.

plot_prevalence(lca)

Replication of the maximum

The likelihood of latent class models often has several local maxima. The "starts" table reports the maximum reached from each start.

get_results(lca, "starts")
#>    start log_likelihood converged iterations error boundary
#> 1      1          -7686      TRUE        315  <NA>    FALSE
#> 2      2          -7686      TRUE        254  <NA>    FALSE
#> 3      3          -7686      TRUE        325  <NA>    FALSE
#> 4      4          -7731      TRUE        323  <NA>    FALSE
#> 5      5          -7695      TRUE        108  <NA>    FALSE
#> 6      6          -7731      TRUE        503  <NA>    FALSE
#> 7      7          -7706      TRUE        158  <NA>    FALSE
#> 8      8          -7719      TRUE        109  <NA>    FALSE
#> 9      9          -7686      TRUE        147  <NA>    FALSE
#> 10    10          -7686      TRUE        262  <NA>    FALSE
#> 11    11          -7686      TRUE        203  <NA>    FALSE
#> 12    12          -7703      TRUE         80  <NA>    FALSE
#> 13    13          -7686      TRUE        147  <NA>    FALSE
#> 14    14          -7686      TRUE        116  <NA>    FALSE
#> 15    15          -7686      TRUE        299  <NA>    FALSE
#> 16    16          -7678      TRUE         81  <NA>    FALSE
#> 17    17          -7704      TRUE        163  <NA>    FALSE
#> 18    18          -7678      TRUE         75  <NA>    FALSE
#> 19    19          -7686      TRUE        122  <NA>    FALSE
#> 20    20          -7686      TRUE         98  <NA>    FALSE

The best log likelihood, -7678, is reached by 2 of the 20 starts; 11 starts stop at -7686 and the others lower. With few starts, the analysis would report a different solution. The number of starts is therefore part of the specification, and the replication of the best maximum belongs in the report.

Classification 

get_results(lca, "counts")
#>         level class effective_count effective_proportion
#> 1 individuals     1            91.4               0.0354
#> 2 individuals     2          1848.0               0.7157
#> 3 individuals     3           642.6               0.2489
#> 4      groups     1            43.6               0.4357
#> 5      groups     2            56.4               0.5643
get_results(lca, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         3    2582      556.82            0.804
#> 2      groups         2     100        8.48            0.878
get_results(lca, "average_posteriors")
#>          level assigned_class class n_assigned average_posterior
#> 1  individuals              1     1         92          9.91e-01
#> 2  individuals              1     2         92          1.42e-09
#> 3  individuals              1     3         92          8.69e-03
#> 4  individuals              2     1       1896          2.45e-10

#> 12      groups              2     1         58          4.80e-02
#> 13      groups              2     2         58          9.52e-01

The classes hold 91.4, 1,848.0 and 642.6 prompts and the group classes 43.6 and 56.4 students. Relative entropy (Ramaswamy et al., 1993) is 0.804 for the prompts and 0.878 for the students. The average posterior of the assigned class is 0.991 for the job class, 0.930 for low activity and 0.858 for media use, and 0.971 and 0.952 for the group classes: the media class overlaps most with low activity, and analyses of assigned classes should use the three-step methods below.

Local independence

The "residuals" table compares the association of each pair of items within each class with the association the model implies (none), with Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

head(get_results(lca, "residuals"), 6)
#>     profile       indicator_1 indicator_2        kind observed expected residual effective_n
#> 1 profile_1   on_social_media     walking categorical    0.424 1.60e-16    0.424        91.4
#> 2 profile_3            sports     walking categorical    0.166 3.80e-17    0.166       642.6
#> 3 profile_3 time_with_friends     walking categorical    0.143 1.45e-17    0.143       642.6
#> 4 profile_3    listened_music     walking categorical    0.133 7.66e-17    0.133       642.6
#> 5 profile_3    listened_music     reading categorical    0.110 8.70e-17    0.110       642.6
#> 6 profile_3    listened_music      sports categorical    0.108 1.42e-16    0.108       642.6
#>   statistic df  p_value p_adjusted
#> 1     16.43  1 5.04e-05    0.00141
#> 2     17.73  1 2.55e-05    0.00107
#> 3     13.21  1 2.79e-04    0.00585
#> 4     11.38  1 7.43e-04    0.01040
#> 5      7.75  1 5.38e-03    0.05022
#> 6      7.52  1 6.09e-03    0.05118

Walking remains associated with sports, time with friends and music within the media class (residuals of 0.13 to 0.17, adjusted p-values 0.001 to 0.010), and with social media within the small job class. local_dependence estimates the joint distribution of a pair of categorical items within each class, as in Latent GOLD.

dependent <- multilca(student_esm, vars = activities, id = "student",
                      n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2,
                      local_dependence = "sports:walking", n_starts = 20,
                      tol = 1e-10, seed = 1)
compare_models(independent = lca, dependent = dependent)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model        Classes  Group classes   k    LogLik       BIC  ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8  Group entropy  Group min AvePP
#> -----------  -------  -------------  --  --------  --------  ----  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----  -------------  ---------------
#> independent        3              2  29  -7678.14  15489.84  5.63   0.056  16640.78     0.80       0.86      0           0.88             0.95
#> dependent          3              2  32  -7668.42  15484.21  0.00   0.944  16618.24     0.81       0.84      0           0.89             0.96

Freeing the pair lowers the BIC by 5.6. The gain is small, the solution is reached by a single start, and the classes keep their meaning, so the model with independent items is retained and the residual association reported.

Uncertainty of the estimates

Several response probabilities of the job class lie on the bound of zero or one, where Wald inference is undefined. boundary = "fix" holds them at the bound and reports every other parameter conditional on them, as in Mplus; the fixed_at_bound attribute names the held parameters.

inference <- parameter_inference(lca, boundary = "fix")
attr(inference, "fixed_at_bound")
#>  [1] "measurement.response.profile_1.tv_video_games:no" 
#>  [2] "measurement.response.profile_1.tv_video_games:yes"
#>  [3] "measurement.response.profile_1.listened_music:no" 
#>  [4] "measurement.response.profile_1.listened_music:yes"
#>  [5] "measurement.response.profile_1.sports:no"

#> [10] "measurement.response.profile_2.part_time_job:yes"
tail(inference, 8)

Ten probabilities are held, both answers of five item–class pairs: TV or video games, music, sports and the job in the job class, and the job in the low-activity class. Group class 1 holds 0.436 of the students (95% interval 0.320 to 0.559), and the probability of a media prompt in that class is 0.529 (0.463 to 0.594).

Relating the classes to affect

three_step() compares the mean of a variable across classes with the BCH correction for classification error (Bolck et al., 2004; Vermunt, 2010).

three_step(lca, data = student_esm, outcome = "happy", contrast = "pairs")
#> Distal outcome: class differences (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class  vs  Difference         95% CI     p  p (BH)
#> -----  --  ----------  -------------  ----  ------
#>     2   1        0.53  [ 0.13, 0.94]  .010    .029
#>     3   1        0.19  [-0.42, 0.79]  .541    .541
#>     3   2       -0.35  [-0.86, 0.17]  .189    .284

Students report higher happiness at low-activity prompts than at job prompts (difference 0.53 on the 1 to 7 scale, 95% interval 0.13 to 0.94, adjusted p = .029). Media prompts do not differ significantly from either class.

Mixed, ordinal and count indicators

multilpa() combines categorical indicators, listed in categorical, with continuous ones. The model below adds three affect ratings as continuous indicators. worried is omitted: half of its ratings are 1, and a Gaussian component for that floor reaches the variance bound.

mixed <- multilpa(student_esm,
                  vars = c("happy", "relaxed", "exhausted", activities),
                  categorical = activities, id = "student", n_profiles = 3,
                  n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
#> Warning: A variance reached min_variance; this is a bound-active constrained fit.
mixed
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 3 profiles, 2 group classes
#> 2582 individuals in 100 groups; varying diagonal residual covariance (VVI), 8 categorical indicators
#> Log likelihood: -18531.292688 | AIC: 37156.585 | BIC (groups): 37279.028
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 39 | best log likelihood reached by 6 of 10 starts (10 converged)
#> A variance is at its specified lower bound.
#> Smallest standardized Gaussian eigenvalue: 7.725e-07 (profiles, profile_2); Gaussian mass: 522.5; weight effective n: 524.7.
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 45.2% (1167)   profile_2 20.2% (522)   profile_3 34.6% (892)
#> Group classes group_class_1 34.9% (35)   group_class_2 65.1% (65)
#> 
#> Means
#>  indicator profile_1 profile_2 profile_3
#>      happy      5.60      5.97      3.31
#>    relaxed      5.23      5.77      3.16
#>  exhausted      3.39      1.00      4.57
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles").
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

The affect ratings dominate the classes: the means separate a low-affect class (happy 3.31, exhausted 4.57) from two positive ones, and the variance of exhausted in one class reaches its bound (min_variance), as the warning reports. Indicators with more information define the classes, so variables that are to be explained by the classes, as affect is here, are better related to them with three_step() than added as indicators.

Ordinal ratings can be modelled as ordinal: an adjacent-category logit with category intercepts shared across classes and a location per class, instead of six free probabilities per item and class (identifying constraints in ?multilpa).

affect <- c("happy", "relaxed", "worried", "exhausted")
ordinal <- multilpa(student_esm, vars = c(affect, activities),
                    id = "student", ordinal = affect,
                    categorical = activities, n_profiles = 3,
                    n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
head(get_results(ordinal, "ordinal"), 7)
#>   profile indicator category probability location location_standard_error
#> 1       1     happy        1    0.197605     -3.4                   0.168
#> 2       1     happy        2    0.227278     -3.4                   0.168
#> 3       1     happy        3    0.312766     -3.4                   0.168
#> 4       1     happy        4    0.182318     -3.4                   0.168
#> 5       1     happy        5    0.072647     -3.4                   0.168
#> 6       1     happy        6    0.007099     -3.4                   0.168
#> 7       1     happy        7    0.000287     -3.4                   0.168

The "ordinal" table gives the fitted probability of each category and the location of each class. Count indicators, such as numbers of messages or absences, are listed in count: Poisson by default, with one mean per class (get_results(fit, "count_means")), or negative binomial (count_model = "negative_binomial") for overdispersion, with class-specific or common (count_dispersion = "equal") dispersion.

Options of multilca()

  • Item types. Binary, ordinal and nominal items share one parameterization, unrestricted category probabilities in each class. Numeric, integer, logical, character and factor columns are accepted; factor levels keep their order, other types are sorted. Ordered items can instead be modelled as ordinal and counts as count (above).
  • Mixed measurement. Continuous and categorical indicators in one model, through multilpa() with categorical.
  • Missing answers. missing = "fiml" uses the observed answers of each row.
  • Bounds. min_probability keeps every response probability above a lower bound.
  • Standard errors. Observed-information and robust (vcov_type = "robust") standard errors through parameter_inference().
  • Model comparison. enumerate_classes() and bootstrap_lrt(); in a FIML fit the bootstrap keeps each row’s pattern of missing answers.
  • Membership covariates. profile_covariates and group_covariates work with categorical indicators, and parameter_inference() reports their standard errors.
  • External variables. three_step() and r3step() work on a categorical fit.
  • Transitions. lta() accepts categorical indicators.

Other functions 

get_results(lca, "classification")      # class sizes and average posteriors
get_results(lca, "responses")           # response probabilities with standard errors
r3step(lca, data = student_esm, covariates = "day")  # membership regressed on a predictor
enumerate_classes(student_esm, vars = activities, categorical = activities,
                  id = "student", n_profiles = 2:4,
                  n_group_classes = 1:3, n_starts = 20, tol = 1e-10,
                  seed = 1)              # compare numbers of classes (slow)
plot_profiles(mixed)                    # means of the continuous indicators
plot_responses(mixed)                   # probabilities of the categorical ones
multilca(student_esm, vars = activities, id = "student", n_profiles = 3,
         n_group_classes = 2, missing = "fiml")  # incomplete answers

Assumptions

  • Items are independent within a class, unless freed with local_dependence.
  • Under unrestricted categorical measurement, each item has its own response distribution in every class; rare responses can produce estimates at the lower bound (min_probability).
  • Prompts are independent given the student’s class; their order within a day or across days is not modelled.
  • Categories are taken from the observed values; factor levels keep their order.

Reporting

A report of a two-level LCA states the items and their coding, the grouping variable, the candidates compared and the criteria used, the number of starts and the replication of the best log likelihood, the response probabilities and class probabilities with intervals, parameters held at bounds, relative entropy and average posteriors at both levels, residual associations, and the method used for external variables.
